wine.name: Don Anselmo
wine.classification: Superiore DOCG on the house's later sheets; earlier vintages carry the Aglianico del Vulture DOC
wine.grapes: Aglianico alone, from old vines of the house's Barile vineyards.
wine.sites: Old vines in the Gelosia district of Barile, by the house's sheets, at about 600 metres on the volcanic slopes of Monte Vulture, the extinct volcano of northern Basilicata.
wine.making: Fermented on its skins in stainless steel for fifteen to eighteen days, with pumping over and délestage. By the house's later sheets it then spends about two years in wood, half in large Slavonian oak casks and half in French barriques used once before, and a year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Sour black cherry, plum and dried violet over tar, smoke and liquorice, with an ashy, savoury edge; full and firm, with high acidity and dense, grippy tannin that grow silkier with age.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed on release, it needs most of a decade to open and lasts for decades in a strong vintage, as the house's tastings of its old vintages show.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead and an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named in honour of the founder, who first sold the family's wine in bottle in 1925.
The DOCG of 2010: at least three years of ageing, twelve months in wood and twelve in bottle.
The Vulture village where the house has made its wine since 1925, its cellars cut into tuff.

records.table: Paternoster's Don Anselmo is Aglianico del Vulture from old vines high on the volcano at Barile, aged about two years in large casks and barriques. Black cherry, tar and smoke ride on high acidity and firm tannin, so decant it and give it years.
records.story: Paternoster dates itself to 1925, when the founder began to sell his Aglianico in bottles under the family's name at Barile, a village on the slopes of Monte Vulture whose cellars are cut into the soft volcanic tuff. For decades the house made the dark, firm, long aged Aglianico of the old Vulture school. Aglianico del Vulture became a DOC in 1971, and in 1985 the family made the first Don Anselmo, named in the founder's honour and drawn from old vines on the hills around Barile, Gelosia among them. It became the house's flagship, given about two years in wood and a year in bottle before it leaves the cellar. A single vineyard red, Rotondo, joined it later in a more modern style. In 2010 the zone's longer aged wine was raised to the Aglianico del Vulture Superiore DOCG, and the house's later sheets print Superiore on Don Anselmo. In August 2016 the Tommasi family of Valpolicella took a majority of the house, and in 2025 Paternoster marked its century with tastings of old vintages of Don Anselmo. To a sommelier it is the long standing reference of the Vulture: Aglianico from volcanic slopes, built to be kept.

others.name: Rotondo
others.note: A single vineyard Aglianico del Vulture of the house, more modern in style than Don Anselmo.

traps: Don Anselmo is Aglianico del Vulture from Basilicata, not Taurasi: the same grape, but Barile lies on Monte Vulture, far from Campania's Irpinia.
A Don Anselmo made before 2010 cannot be Superiore DOCG, because the DOCG dates from 2010; older bottles are Aglianico del Vulture DOC.
Rotondo is a separate single vineyard wine of the house, not a second wine of Don Anselmo.

cards.front: Paternoster's Don Anselmo: whom does the name honour, and what is its first vintage?
cards.back: The founder, who began bottling under the family's name in 1925; the first Don Anselmo is the 1985 vintage.

cards.front: How is Don Anselmo aged, by the house's later sheets?
cards.back: About two years in wood, half in large Slavonian oak casks and half in once used French barriques, then a year in bottle.

questions.q: A guest asks what the word Superiore on a later bottle of Paternoster's Don Anselmo promises. Which answer fits?

Grapes from the volcano's upper slopes alone
Five years in large old casks before release
A share of Merlot blended in for softness
questions.exp: The Aglianico del Vulture Superiore DOCG of 2010 asks for three years of ageing with twelve months in wood and twelve in bottle; five years is the rule for the Riserva.

The Antinori family of Florence
The Mastroberardino family of Atripalda
The Librandi family of Cirò Marina

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, with one more on the Superiore rules shared by the group; no fetch tried for this house.

The plan's note is answered: the house's sheet for the 2016 vintage names Don Anselmo Aglianico del Vulture Superiore, while its product page and trade listings of the 2015 vintage say DOC, so the classification says Superiore on the later sheets and DOC before; WineNews lists the 2016 vintage once as DOC and once as DOCG.
The 2015 sheet gives a different cellar: half fermented in steel and half in oak, twenty months in wood and six in steel; the record follows the 2016 sheet and hedges it as the later sheets.

The first Don Anselmo of 1985 rests on WineNews and Gambero Rosso International; WineNews calls it the founder's son's tribute to his father, while Gambero Rosso has a grandson recall making it with his brothers, so the record says the family.

The founder is described, not named: he was born in 1896 by Gambero Rosso and in 1898 by another account, and no source gave the year of his death; his son, said to have trained at Conegliano, rests on one source and is left out.

The Tommasi majority of August 2016 rests on WineNews's report of 2016, the Corriere del Vino and the Tommasi group's own page; Rotondo's first vintage is 1997 in one review and 1998 in the Corriere, so no year is given, and the new winery of 2006 and the move to Slavonian oak rest on WineNews alone and are left out.
Synthesi, the house's younger Aglianico, named in 1997 by two accounts, is left out of others for want of a sixth source slot.
The library's founding year of 1925 and its tuff cellars agree with every source read.

wine.name: Titolo
wine.grapes: Aglianico alone, from the estate's own old vines.
wine.sites: The highest part of Contrada Solagna del Titolo at Barile, at about 600 metres at the foot of Monte Vulture, on layers of lava, lapilli and ash laid down by the volcano and alternating with clay.
wine.making: After fermentation the wine goes into French barriques of about two hundred litres, half of them new, where it completes its malolactic fermentation. It then ages at least a year in barrique, two on the house's newest page, and a further year in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Black cherry, blackberry and violet over ash, graphite and a touch of cocoa from the barrel; dense yet fresh, with bright acidity, fine, firm tannin and a long, smoky finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and tight when young, it opens after five to eight years and holds well beyond a decade in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: From Contrada Solagna del Titolo, the vineyard district at Barile; the word is a place, not a rank.
The DOC for Aglianico grown on the slopes of Monte Vulture in northern Basilicata.

records.table: Titolo is the one wine the Elena Fucci estate staked everything on: Aglianico del Vulture from the high Titolo vineyard at Barile, on lava, ash and clay at the foot of the volcano. Black cherry, violet and smoke over bright acidity; decant it an hour ahead.
records.story: The vineyards behind this estate were bought in the 1960s by the founder's grandfather, who chose the highest part of Contrada Solagna del Titolo at Barile, at the foot of the extinct volcano of Monte Vulture. By 2000 the family meant to sell them: the vines were too much to keep for pleasure, and the children were expected to leave home for university. At the last moment the founder, then a student of viticulture and oenology, could not accept that the vineyard she had grown up in, holding by the house's account some of the oldest vines on the Vulture, would pass to another name. The family kept the land, the estate began with the 2000 vintage, and from the first it put everything into a single wine named for the vineyard, Titolo. An outside consultant helped at first; from 2004 the founder ran every part of the estate herself, in the vineyard and in the cellar. Titolo ages in French barriques and then in bottle, and the house has since added a Riserva from the same vineyard. To a sommelier it is a lesson in what one high, old vineyard on Vulture's volcanic ash and clay can give to Aglianico, and a reminder that a young estate can carry an old vineyard's name.

others.name: Titolo Riserva
others.note: A Riserva from the same vineyard, which the house lists beside the classic Titolo.

traps: Titolo is Aglianico del Vulture of Basilicata, grown on volcanic soils; Taurasi is the Aglianico DOCG of Campania.
Titolo names the vineyard district, Contrada Solagna del Titolo, not a title or rank of the wine.
Titolo is the estate's single founding wine, not one cru among many: the house began in 2000 with that one label.

cards.front: Elena Fucci's Titolo: what does the name refer to?
cards.back: Contrada Solagna del Titolo, the vineyard district at Barile on Monte Vulture where its Aglianico grows.

cards.front: What happened to the vineyards behind Titolo in 2000?
cards.back: The family was about to sell them; the founder kept them instead, and the first Titolo is the 2000 vintage.

questions.q: A guest reads the word Titolo on a bottle of Aglianico from the Elena Fucci estate. What does it tell them?
opts: The vineyard district at Barile where it grows
A rank above Superiore in the Vulture's rules
The year the estate's vines were planted
A blend drawn from several Vulture villages
questions.exp: Titolo is taken from Contrada Solagna del Titolo, the vineyard district at Barile; it is no rank, and the wine comes from that one site rather than a blend of villages.

questions.q: Which choice of the year 2000 began the estate that makes Titolo at Barile?
opts: The family kept its old vineyard instead of selling it
The family bought tuff caves once used by friars
A co-operative of Barile split into small estates
A Campanian house planted new vines on Vulture
questions.exp: By the house's account the family was about to sell the vineyard in 2000 when the founder chose to keep it; the first Titolo is the 2000 vintage.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, three of them on the house's own domain; a fetch of the house's history page was refused (the host does not resolve here) and not retried.

The house carries the name of its living founder, so she is never named in prose; her grandfather, who bought the vineyards in the 1960s, is described and not named, since the house's pages speak of him as living at different ages and no source gives his dates.
The plan's note is answered: Contrada Solagna del Titolo at Barile is on the house's history page and its brochure, at about 600 metres by its Titolo pages.

The house's pages differ on the barrel time: the wine club page gives twelve months in barriques of two hundred litres, half new, with the malolactic there and twelve months in bottle; the Titolo Classico page gives twenty four months, so the record says at least a year, two on the newest page.

The house now lists the wine as Titolo Classico beside a Titolo Riserva and a Titolo by Amphora; one merchant lists a 2020 Titolo as Superiore DOCG, which no second source confirmed, so the record gives the DOC, which Falstaff and the house's pages show.

Left out for want of a second source: the barrel cellar dug into the hillside beneath the family home, the organic certification, the founder's studies at Pisa and her return in 2005 (the house says she ran the estate from 2004), and the vines' ages, which are volatile.
The library calls Titolo a single high vineyard; the house speaks of its vineyards in Contrada Solagna del Titolo, so the record speaks of the highest part of that district rather than one parcel.

records.place: Rionero in Vulture, Aglianico del Vulture, Basilicata

wine.name: La Firma
wine.grapes: Aglianico alone, picked late in the season.
wine.sites: The family's own vineyards of Aglianico on the volcanic slopes of Monte Vulture; the wine ages in the house's tuff caves in the centre of Rionero in Vulture.
wine.making: Picked in the first ten days of November, macerated for about twenty days and fermented in stainless steel. It then ages at least twelve months in new French barriques, kept in the volcanic tuff caves beneath Rionero, and a further twelve months in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Deep ruby with garnet glints; blackberry, black cherry and plum with liquorice, cocoa and vanilla from the new oak; ripe and full, with fresh acidity, firm tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Ripe and approachable a few years after release, it softens and gains savoury depth over the following decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; decant an hour ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Italian for the signature, the last act of a notarial deed, after which the house names this wine.
The notary's cellars: a name that honours the founder's father, a notary at Rionero.
The DOC for Aglianico grown on the slopes of Monte Vulture in northern Basilicata.

records.table: Cantine del Notaio's La Firma, the signature, is Aglianico del Vulture picked in early November and aged a year in new barriques in tuff caves beneath Rionero. Ripe blackberry and liquorice over firm tannin: decant it and pour it with roast lamb or game.
records.story: Cantine del Notaio was founded in 1998 at Rionero in Vulture by a graduate in agricultural science and his wife, to make Aglianico del Vulture from the family's own vineyards. By the house's account the family had worked vines on the Vulture for seven generations, and the founder's grandfather, whose name he shared, left those vineyards to him. The house's name, the notary's cellars, honours the notary of the family, the founder's father, who began work as a notary at Rionero in 1959, and its wines take their names from a notary's office: Il Preliminare, Il Repertorio, Il Sigillo, Il Rogito and La Firma, the signature at the foot of a deed. The house brought back into use its own caves in the centre of Rionero, cut into the volcanic tuff in the seventeenth century, by its account, and used by Franciscan friars; they hold the barriques in which La Firma ages. La Firma comes from Aglianico picked in the first days of November, aged a year in new French oak and a year in bottle. To a sommelier it shows the Vulture in a riper, oak framed style beside the long aged Aglianico of neighbouring Barile, and why the zone digs its cellars rather than building them.

others.name: Il Repertorio
others.note: Another Aglianico del Vulture of the house, named for the notary's register of deeds.

others.name: Il Sigillo
others.note: A further Aglianico del Vulture of the house, named for the notary's seal.

traps: La Firma is the house's name for the wine, the signature; it is no rank, and the wine is Aglianico del Vulture DOC, not Superiore.
Cantine del Notaio lies at Rionero in Vulture beside Barile, in Basilicata; its tuff caves are a Vulture landmark, not a Campanian one.
The house's caves hold the barriques; the vineyards lie outside the village, on the slopes of the volcano.

cards.back: The signature, the last act of a notarial deed: the house's wines take a notary's words, after the founder's father, a notary.

cards.front: Where does La Firma spend its year in new barriques?
cards.back: In caves cut into the tuff beneath the centre of Rionero in Vulture, dug in the seventeenth century and once used by Franciscan friars.

Dried Aglianico grapes pressed for a sweet red
Aglianico and Merlot aged in large old casks

questions.q: Why do the wines of Cantine del Notaio at Rionero in Vulture carry names such as La Firma and Il Repertorio?

They recall deeds of sale of old Vulture vineyards

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's 35, two on the house's own domain; no fetch tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1998 is on the house's La Storia page and on Superiore.de, Vinorandum and other trade profiles; La Firma is Aglianico del Vulture DOC on the house's sheet and every trade listing read (vintages 2005 to 2018), with no Superiore DOCG bottling found.

The founder and his wife are living and are described, not named; the notary of the house's Il Notaio vero page, who began to practise at Rionero on 4 June 1959, is the founder's father by Superiore.de and by a trade profile (UR Italian Wines), and is not named since no source gave his dates.

The caves of the seventeenth century used by Franciscan friars are on the house's grottoes page, and also on the listing of the Associazione Dimore Storiche Italiane and on Italian Botanical Heritage, neither cited for want of a slot; the house says the caves date back to 1600, which the record reads as the seventeenth century.

The house's sheet gives the harvest in the first ten days of November, about twenty days of maceration, steel, first passage French barriques for at least twelve months and twelve months in bottle, and 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a merchant adds slightly overripe grapes picked by hand, which the record leaves out.

Left out for want of a second source or as volatile: La Firma's first vintage (no source found), the vineyard area (26 to 52 hectares by source), the number of communes, the farming method and the consultant oenologist, who is living.

Il Repertorio and Il Sigillo as Aglianico del Vulture rest on Superiore.de's listings; the region record's producers line agrees that the house makes Aglianico del Vulture in several styles. The caves' cool, damp air all year rests on the heritage listing alone and is cut.

wine.name: Duca Sanfelice
wine.classification: Rosso Classico Superiore Riserva of the Cirò DOC, aged at least two years
wine.grapes: Gaglioppo alone, from old bush vines.
wine.sites: The Duca Sanfelice vineyard at Ponta, planted by the founder in the 1950s by the house's account: old bush vines of Gaglioppo, trained as alberello, on clay and limestone in the Cirò Classico zone.
wine.making: Picked in the first ten days of October and fermented in stainless steel, with seven to ten days on the skins. It then rests two years in stainless steel, with no wood, and a few months in bottle before release, by the house's sheet.
wine.glass: Pale garnet with an orange rim; red cherry, wild strawberry and orange peel over dried herbs, liquorice and a hint of tar; medium bodied but firm, with lively acidity and dry, grippy tannin.
wine.ageing: Ready from about three years after the harvest, by the house's sheet, it keeps for more than ten years, turning towards dried cherry, leather and tobacco.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle gently off its sediment; a Burgundy glass, which suits its pale colour and perfume.

label.means: The name of the family's vineyard at Ponta, as the house spells it, in one word.
Red from the historic core of the Cirò zone, the heart of the appellation.
At least 13.5 per cent alcohol and at least two years of ageing before release, by the Cirò rules.

records.table: Librandi's Duca Sanfelice is Cirò Rosso Classico Superiore Riserva from old bush vines of Gaglioppo, aged two years in steel rather than wood. Pale in the glass yet firm, with red cherry, orange peel and dried herbs; pour it with Calabrian salumi or roast lamb.
records.story: Librandi traces its roots to the vineyard at Ponta that the founder planted in the 1950s, by the house's account, and in 1953 the family began to bottle wine in a small cellar on Via Tirone at Cirò Marina. Cirò became a DOC in 1969. The founder's two sons built the house together for some forty years, one at the making and selling of the wines, the other at the cellar, the staff and the accounts, and in 1975 they opened a new winery in Contrada San Gennaro on the coast road at Cirò Marina. In 1988 the house released its first Gravello, which joins Gaglioppo to Cabernet Sauvignon and which it calls its flagship. From 1993 the family planted experimental vineyards to save Calabria's forgotten grapes, Magliocco and Mantonico among them. The brothers led the house until 2012, when the next generation took charge, and in 2025 Cirò Classico became Calabria's first DOCG. Duca Sanfelice, pure Gaglioppo from the founder's vines aged in steel rather than wood, is the house's Cirò in its classic form, and the bottle a sommelier reaches for to teach the appellation.

others.name: Gravello
others.note: Gaglioppo with Cabernet Sauvignon, labelled IGT Calabria and first released in 1988; the wine the house itself calls its flagship.

traps: Duca Sanfelice is aged in steel, not oak: its pale colour and dry grip come from Gaglioppo itself, not from barrels.
Duca Sanfelice is labelled Cirò DOC Rosso Classico Superiore Riserva; Cirò Classico DOCG, which asks for six months in wood, dates only from 2025.
Gravello, Gaglioppo with Cabernet Sauvignon, is the wine Librandi calls its flagship; Duca Sanfelice is its Cirò of Gaglioppo alone.

report: Searches for this record: 8 of the group's 35, five on the house's own domain; no fetch tried.

A swap for the checker to rule on: the house's own Gravello page calls Gravello the flagship wine of the company, so by the brief's rule the house's flagship is Gravello (IGT Calabria, Gaglioppo with Cabernet Sauvignon), not Duca Sanfelice; the record keeps the plan's Duca Sanfelice, chosen in the plan's note to teach Cirò, says plainly that the house calls Gravello its flagship, and proposes either keeping it so or a swap to Gravello under a new key.
The plan's note on the spelling is answered: the house writes Duca Sanfelice in one word; its importer and Decanter's older reviews write Duca San Felice, and Decanter's newer reviews Duca Sanfelice.

Founded is empty: trade accounts give 1950 for the founding, the house and Gambero Rosso give 1953 for the first bottling in Via Tirone, and the founder planted Ponta in the 1950s by the house; the founder and his two sons are described, not named, since no source gave their dates and a living grandson shares the founder's name.

The Duca Sanfelice sheet gives Gaglioppo from old alberello vines on clay and limestone, the harvest in the first ten days of October, seven to ten days on the skins in steel, two years in steel and a few months in bottle, ready from three years and keeping more than ten; the Ponta vineyard as the Duca Sanfelice estate is on the house's pages and the importer's, which also calls it the family's oldest vineyard and the last the founder planted, a claim left out on one source.

Cirò's DOC of 1969 and the Superiore and Riserva rules rest on Decanter's regional profile and the AIS copy of the rules; the DOCG of 2025 rests on DoctorWine's report of the European Union's registration and the region record's refuted law, and DoctorWine says the Classico Superiore stays within the DOC.

Left out for want of a source slot or a second source: the professor of the University of Milan beside the house's survey and the Rosaneti collection of some two hundred varieties planted in a spiral (both on the house's research page, not cited), the first Magno Megonio of 1995 (one page of the house calls Megonio a Gaglioppo, another a Magliocco Dolce) and the clones registered in 2014.

The brothers' roles and the handover of 2012 are on the house's history pages, the roles on its page in memory of one brother; the house's timeline says the first vintages of Gravello were released in 1988, so the record says released in 1988 rather than naming a vintage. The region record's producers line (Magliocco among the grapes revived) agrees with the house's pages.

records.place: Bianco and Casignana, Greco di Bianco, Calabria

wine.name: Greco di Bianco
wine.grapes: Greco Bianco, at least ninety five per cent by the DOC's rules: the local vine long called Greco di Gerace.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the DOC's small zone on the Ionian coast of Reggio Calabria, the commune of Bianco and part of neighbouring Casignana, near the tip of Calabria's toe.
wine.making: After the harvest the bunches are dried, in the sun on cane mats or in ventilated drying rooms as the DOC allows, until they have lost up to about a third of their weight. The shrivelled grapes are then pressed and fermented into a sweet wine, with the vintage printed on every label.
wine.glass: Gold to amber; dried apricot, fig and candied orange peel with honey, almond and a hint of bitter herbs; sweet and full, with a fresh acidity that keeps the finish clean.
wine.ageing: Generous when young, it keeps for years in a cool cellar as its fruit turns towards dried apricot, toasted nuts and caramel.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, a little warmer for an old bottle; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, poured in modest measures.

label.means: The DOC of 1980 for sweet wine of dried Greco Bianco from Bianco and part of Casignana.
Made from grapes dried after picking: the only type of wine the Greco di Bianco DOC allows.

records.table: Ceratti's Greco di Bianco is a sweet passito from near the tip of Calabria's toe, made from Greco Bianco grapes dried after picking until they shrivel. Apricot, candied orange and almond on a fresh finish: pour it cool with almond pastries or blue cheese.
records.story: Greco di Bianco takes its name from Bianco, a small town on the Ionian coast of Reggio Calabria, and the word Greco, Greek, is given in Calabria to several vines that are not related. The grape of this wine was long known as Greco di Gerace, after the old town of the same coast. On 18 June 1980 a decree made Greco di Bianco a DOC, the first of the province of Reggio Calabria, and its rules allow a single wine: a passito of at least ninety five per cent Greco Bianco from Bianco and part of neighbouring Casignana, the vintage on every label and no Superiore or Riserva. In 2006 a DNA study found that Greco di Gerace shares its genetic profile with Malvasia delle Lipari and Malvasia di Sardegna, and with Malvasias of Spain and Croatia, so the vine is an old variety met across the Mediterranean under other names. Ceratti is a family estate of the zone, known for this one wine, which it bottles under a white label and a black. To a sommelier the wine is a rare taste of the sweet tradition of Calabria's toe, and a lesson that a name such as Greco can mislead.

others.name: Greco di Bianco Black Label
others.note: The house's second bottling of Greco di Bianco, listed beside the White Label.

traps: Greco di Bianco is a sweet passito of Calabria; Greco di Tufo is a dry white DOCG of Campania.
Bianco is the name of the town, not the colour: Greco di Bianco means the Greco of Bianco.
By a DNA study of 2006 the vine of Greco di Bianco shares its profile with Malvasia delle Lipari, whatever its name says.

cards.front: Ceratti's Greco di Bianco: how are the grapes treated before pressing?
cards.back: Dried after picking, in the sun on cane mats or in ventilated rooms, until they lose up to about a third of their weight.

cards.front: What did a DNA study of 2006 find about the vine behind Greco di Bianco, the wine Ceratti makes?
cards.back: Greco di Gerace, its old name, shares its profile with Malvasia delle Lipari and Malvasia di Sardegna.

questions.q: A guest is offered Ceratti's Greco di Bianco after dinner. Which describes the wine in the glass?
opts: A sweet white of dried Greco Bianco grapes
A dry white of Greco from Campania's hills
A fortified white aged in a solera
A late picked red of Gaglioppo
questions.exp: Greco di Bianco is a passito: Greco Bianco grapes dried after picking, then pressed and fermented sweet; the dry Greco of Campania's hills is Greco di Tufo.

questions.q: In which year did Greco di Bianco, the wine Ceratti makes, become a DOC, the first of the province of Reggio Calabria?
questions.exp: The decree recognising Greco di Bianco is dated 18 June 1980, by the DOC's own rules, which call it the first DOC of the province of Reggio Calabria.

report: Searches for this record: 9 of the group's 35, two of them on the DOC's rules; no fetch tried, and no site of the house was found.

A thin pick, said plainly: the house's own facts (its place at Contrada Palazzi in Casignana on the coast road, its family run from a founder through his son to his grandson, and its White Label and Black Label) rest on the Wine Scholar Guild's producer guide alone, with a writer's wiki the brief does not allow as a source agreeing; the checker should confirm or cut them, and if they cannot be confirmed the merge agent should look for a better documented house of Greco di Bianco or of Calabria.

So the place gives the DOC's zone, Bianco and Casignana, rather than the estate's village, the founding year is empty (the guide says the early 1900s, the wiki 1958) and the story names no person or date of the house.

The DOC's facts (the decree of 18 June 1980, the first of the province, at least 95 per cent Greco Bianco, the zone, drying in the sun on cane mats or by forced air with a loss of up to 35 per cent of weight, the passito the only type, no Superiore or Riserva and the vintage required) rest on the AIS copy of the rules.

The DNA match of Greco di Gerace with Malvasia delle Lipari, Malvasia di Sardegna, Malvasia de Sitges and Malvasia dubrovačka rests on the VITIS paper of 2006 and the Wein-plus glossary, which also gives Greco Bianco di Gerace as the vine of the Greco di Bianco DOC and notes that other Calabrian vines called Greco Bianco are different grapes.

The region record's grapes line calls Greco Bianco the white of Cirò Bianco and of Greco di Bianco alike; by the sources read the Greco di Bianco vine is the Malvasia delle Lipari genotype and other Calabrian Greco Bianco vines are distinct, so whether Cirò's Greco Bianco is the same vine is in tension and is reported, not settled.

Left out for want of a second source: the Greek settlers said to have brought the vine, the drying time of about ten days, the house's barrique aged Black Label, its seven hectares and bottle count, and the house's place in the DOC's consortium.
